content: The Common Lilac, scientifically known as Syringa vulgaris, is a deciduous plant belonging to the olive family (Oleaceae). It is native to the Balkan Peninsula in southeastern Europe, where it naturally grows in the wild on rocky hills. This plant can take the form of a large shrub or a small tree, typically reaching a height of 6 to 7 meters. Its bark is smooth and ranges in color from gray to gray-brown. The shrubs are multi-stemmed, producing secondary shoots from their base or roots. The leaves of the Common Lilac are simple in structure, light green to glaucous in color, and vary in shape from oval to heart-shaped (cordate). They exhibit pinnate venation, have a mucronate apex, and possess an entire margin. The leaves typically grow to a length of 5 to 10 centimeters and are arranged in opposite pairs or occasionally in whorls of three. The flowers of the Common Lilac are four-petaled and cup-shaped, with a four-lobed corolla. They are most commonly lilac to mauve in color, although variations exist. These flowers are densely arranged in terminal panicles that measure 8 to 18 centimeters in length. The fruit of the plant is a dry, smooth, brown capsule approximately 1 centimeter long. The Common Lilac is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant in gardens and parks due to the attractive and sweet fragrance of its flowers. Most garden varieties are cultivars with flowers that range in color from white to dark lilac. The majority of these garden cultivars do not exceed a height of 4 to 5 meters. Syringa vulgaris has been designated as the state flower of New Hampshire, symbolizing the hardy character of the men and women of the Granite State, as stated in the New Hampshire Revised Statute Annotated (RSA) 3:5. Several notable cultivars of Syringa vulgaris include: Syringa vulgaris 'Alba' Syringa vulgaris 'Charles Joly' Syringa vulgaris 'Corondel' Syringa vulgaris 'Etna' Syringa vulgaris 'Mme. Francisque Morel'
